title: See what people find, then decide what you stand for

say: See what people find, then decide what you stand for.
This is the video for module one of Personal Branding and Online Presence.
A personal brand is what people understand about you, your skills and your character when you are not in the room.
You already have one. Personal branding means making that picture true, clear and easy to find.

panel.heading: You already have a personal brand
items: Clarity: one sentence on what you do
Consistency: same name and photo everywhere
Credibility: real proof of your work

say: Every personal brand has three parts. Clarity: a person can say in one sentence what you do and who you help.

say: Consistency: your name, photo and description match on every platform, so people know it is the same you.

say: Now see yourself the way a stranger does. Set aside 30 minutes.

say: Open a private or incognito tab on your phone, so your own history does not change the results. Search your full name in quotation marks.

say: Give each platform 0 or 1 on five checks. A real, readable name. A clear photo of your face. Can a stranger tell your trade in 5 seconds? Any proof of your work? Is it clear how to reach you?

say: Then circle the platform that matters most for your goal and has the lowest score. That is where you start.

panel.rule: Start with the platform that matters most and scores lowest.

say: For example, Amaka bakes celebration cakes in Lagos and wants orders from people outside her church circle.
On WhatsApp her name shows as Mama Tobi, the photo is her son, and her About line says Busy. She scores 1 out of 5.

cards.d: Name shows 'Mama Tobi', the photo is her son, About says 'Busy'. Only the contact check passes.
Handle @amakacakes and 40 cake posts, but the photo is a cake and there is no clear way to order.
A personal profile whose last cake post was in 2022.

say: Her Instagram does better: a clear handle, 40 cake posts, and a bio. But there is no contact route. 3 out of 5.

cards.d: Name shows 'Mama Tobi', the photo is her son, About says 'Busy'. Only the contact check passes.
Handle @amakacakes and 40 cake posts, but the photo is a cake and there is no clear way to order.
A personal profile whose last cake post was in 2022.

say: Her Facebook scores 1 out of 5, because the last cake post was in 2022.
WhatsApp is where most customers message her, and it scores lowest, so she fixes it first. She keeps every screenshot in an album called Brand before.

say: Next, decide what you want to be known for. Your value proposition is the reason a particular person should choose you.

panel.heading: Four blocks, one sentence
items: Who you help
Their problem or goal
What you offer
Your proof

say: First, who exactly do you help? Not everybody.

panel.heading: Four blocks, one sentence
items: Who you help
Their problem or goal
What you offer
Your proof

say: Second, what do they struggle with or want?

panel.heading: Four blocks, one sentence
items: Who you help
Their problem or goal
What you offer
Your proof

say: Third, what do you do about it?

panel.heading: Four blocks, one sentence
items: Who you help
Their problem or goal
What you offer
Your proof

say: And fourth, why should they believe you? Proof must be specific and checkable, like photos of real work.
Then join the four blocks into one sentence.

panel.heading: Four blocks, one sentence
items: Who you help
Their problem or goal
What you offer
Your proof

say: For example, Halima is a bookkeeper in Kano. Her old profile said: Accountant. Hardworking and reliable. Call me. A reader learns almost nothing.
Her new sentence: I help small shop owners in Kano know their real monthly profit, with simple bookkeeping and a one-page summary every month. Trusted by three local pharmacies.
And never claim clients or results you do not have.
Two strong platforms beat six weak ones, so choose by where your audience is.
And protect your accounts before you share your handle widely, because a public profile attracts scammers too.

panel.heading: Lock your accounts first
items: WhatsApp: turn on two-step verification
Other apps: turn on two-factor authentication
A different strong password for each account
Never share a login code, even with a friend

say: On WhatsApp, go to Settings, Account, Two-step verification, and create a six-digit PIN. Add an email address so you can reset it.

say: On Instagram, Facebook and LinkedIn, open the security settings and turn on two-factor authentication.

say: Use a different strong password for each account, kept somewhere safe.

say: A common fraud is account takeover: someone tricks you into giving a code, then asks your contacts for money in your name. Never share a code, even with someone claiming to be the app, a bank or a friend.

panel.rule: Never share a verification or login code with anyone.

say: Decide now what you will never post publicly. Your home address. Your children's school or uniform. Your daily routine and live location. Photos of ID cards, bank cards or BVN details. And travel plans before you return.
Share a business area, not a house address.

items: Your home address

say: Here is your practice. Run your self-search audit and score each platform. Write your positioning statement in short, medium and long versions, and test it on someone who does not know your work.
Choose your one or two do first platforms, turn on two-step verification, and write your never-post list.
Now continue with the lessons below.
